title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.
key_points: Test loss falls as a power law in model size, dataset size, and compute.
The trends are smooth and span many orders of magnitude.
Larger models are more sample-efficient — they learn more per token of data.
Predictable curves let you forecast performance before training the full model.
Motivated the push toward ever-larger language models.
content_html: Kaplan, McCandlish, and colleagues at OpenAI in 2020 measured how language model loss changes as you scale three things: parameters, training data, and compute. They found loss falls as a clean power law in each, holding across many orders of magnitude. The upshot is that performance becomes surprisingly predictable, which made investing in larger models a reasoned bet rather than a gamble.
extra_html:
How it works

The authors trained many models of varying sizes on varying amounts of data and compute, then plotted the resulting loss. On log-log axes the points fall along straight lines — the signature of a power law. They also found larger models reach a given loss using fewer training tokens, so scaling up the model is an efficient way to spend a compute budget.

Why it matters

Smooth, predictable curves let labs forecast how a big training run will turn out from cheaper small-scale experiments, de-risking expensive projects. This paper provided much of the intellectual justification for the race to scale that followed. It also set the stage for later refinements — notably Chinchilla — which revisited exactly how to balance model size against data.

related.title: GPT-3: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
related.hook: Show the model a few examples right in the prompt and it picks up the task — no fine-tuning, no gradient updates. GPT-3 turned prompting into the new programming.

related.title: Chinchilla: Compute-Optimal Scaling
related.hook: Most giant models were starved of data. Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget you should grow parameters and tokens together — and a smaller, longer-trained model won.
